title_en: Papyrus Fragment against Apollinarius and Nestorius
author: Cyril of Alexandria
occasion: The fragment defends the Nicene faith against two christological errors: the opinion of Apollinarius and the blasphemy of Nestorius. The writer distances himself from both and addresses disturbances in the church.
argument: The author equates the opinion of Apollinarius and the blasphemy of Nestorius as the same impiety. He identifies two errors: attaching division or a duality to the Only-Begotten Son of God according to the incarnation, and not confessing his ensouled and all-holy flesh as human except for sin alone. He holds to the orthodox and unadulterated faith confirmed by the blessed and saving creed of Nicaea. He rejects communion or association with those who hold such errors, citing Scripture that they err not knowing the Scriptures. He denies having imposed anything on the pious, calling such an imposition foolish and senseless, and condemns those who disturb the church and its Christ-loving people.

outline.move: The author identifies Apollinarius's opinion and Nestorius's blasphemy as the same impiety, describing errors about division, duality, and Christ's flesh.
He declares his adherence to the Nicene creed and his refusal of communion or association with those who hold the condemned views.
He denies having imposed anything on the pious, calls such an imposition foolish and senseless, and condemns those who disturb the church and its Christ-loving people.
The fragment breaks off with a reference to condemnation and to natures and forms, but the sentence is incomplete.

scripture: The fragment quotes a saying close to Matthew 22:29 ('You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures'), but with textual variation: the fragment has μὴ εἰδότες where Matthew has οὐκ εἰδότες. No book name is given. LXX conventions are not otherwise evidenced in this fragment.
uncertain: The addressee of the letter is not preserved.
The exact date of composition cannot be established from the fragment.
The precise wording of many lacunose passages is uncertain.
The identity of the persons disturbing the church is not stated.
Whether 'natures and forms' refers to a specific formula or opponents' language is unclear.
The exact form of the scriptural quotation is uncertain due to the lacunose text.

_unresolved_facts.claim: not confessing his ensouled and all-holy flesh as human except for sin alone
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: το την ἐμψυχον αὐτου και παναγιαν σαρκα μ̣η ἀνθρωπινην [ὁ]μ̣ολο̣γειν, π̣λην [ἁμαρ]τ̣ιας μονον χω[ρις
_unresolved_facts.fix: The author says the error is 'not confessing his ensouled and all-holy flesh as human' — the 'except for sin alone' (πλὴν ἁμαρτίας μόνον χωρίς) modifies the orthodox position (Hebrews 4:15), not the error. The error is denying the flesh is human; the 'except for sin alone' is the author's orthodox qualification of Christ's humanity, not part of what the heretics deny.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He identifies two errors: attaching division or a duality to the Only-Begotten Son of God according to the incarnation, and not confessing his ensouled and all-holy flesh as human except for sin alone
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἰσης και [της αὐ]της ἀσεβειας εἰ[ν]αι π̣ι̣στευων, το με[ρ]ι̣σμον ἠ δυαδα τῳ Μονογενει Ὑ(ι)ῳ του Θ(εο)υ κατα την οἰκονομια(ν) π̣ρ̣οσαπτειν, και το την ἐμψυχον αὐτου και παναγιαν σαρκα μ̣η ἀνθρωπινην [ὁ]μ̣ολο̣γειν
_unresolved_facts.fix: The author identifies these as two aspects of 'the same impiety' (ἴσης καὶ [τῆς αὐ]τῆς ἀσεβείας), not two separate errors. The brief should clarify that these are presented as equivalent expressions of one impiety, not two distinct errors.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He denies having imposed anything on the pious, calling such an imposition foolish and senseless
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: οὐτε τοις εὐσ[εβεσι]ν ἐπεσκηψα· εὐη̣[θες γα]ρ και ἀνο̣ητον
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Greek says he has not 'imposed' (ἐπεσκήψα) on the pious, and that doing so would be 'foolish and senseless' — but the brief should note the textual uncertainty: [εὐη̣[θες γα]ρ και ἀνο̣ητον] is heavily restored. The sense is clear but the exact wording is conjectural.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The fragment breaks off with a reference to condemnation and to natures and forms, but the sentence is incomplete
_unresolved_facts.fix: The fragment breaks off with 'φυσεων γαρ και μ̣[ο]ρ̣φων/' — 'of natures and forms' with a paragraphus mark. This is not clearly a 'reference to condemnation and to natures and forms' as two things; rather, the condemnation (κατακεκρι[σθαι]) is stated, and then a new clause about 'natures and forms' begins but breaks off immediately. The 'natures and forms' may be the subject of a new sentence, not a continuation of the condemnation.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Scripture (quoted), introduced by εἰπών and the quotation 'Πλα[νωντ]αι μη εἰδοτες [τ]ας [γρα]φα[ς]'
_unresolved_facts.fix: The quotation is introduced by εἰπών but the syntax is unclear due to lacunae. The form ἐμπεπτω[κ···]ι̣ν suggests a participle or infinitive construction ('having fallen into... saying, They err...'). The 'εἰπών' may not introduce a direct scriptural quotation formula but rather the author's own words characterizing the opponents. The brief should note uncertainty about whether this is a formal scriptural citation or the author's description of the opponents.

_unresolved_facts.claim: the fragment has μὴ εἰδότες where Matthew has οὐκ εἰδότες
_unresolved_facts.fix: The fragment has 'Πλα[νωντ]α̣ι μη εἰδοτες' — the verb is plural ('they err') vs. Matthew's plural ('πλανᾶσθε' — 'you err'). The brief correctly notes μὴ vs. οὐκ, but should also note the person change (3rd person vs. 2nd person). More importantly, the source of this saying is uncertain — it could be Matthew 22:29/Mark 12:24, but the 3rd person form suggests it may be a common Christian saying rather than direct citation.
